diagnosticSigns: superficial white powdery colonies
colony texture extends across multiple leaf regions
USDA caption independently identifies severe powdery mildew

record whether material wipes or transfers

mediaRecords.plant: multiple USDA reference hosts including Brazilian peppertree
mediaRecords.distribution: direct organisms visible; one source shows larvae and adults feeding on the host
mediaRecords.mediumRootZone: not relevant to direct organism morphology
mediaRecords.measuredValues: adult Thrips palmi captioned by USDA at approximately 1.5 mm
diagnosticSigns: slender thrips body morphology
larval and adult life stages visible on host tissue
USDA image identifiers and organism captions
plausibleAlternatives: incidental organism not responsible for a separate plant symptom
mite feeding or residue when no organism body is visible
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Require a sharp direct organism or larval view plus compatible feeding injury or frass before attributing a user's plant damage to thrips.
mediaRecords.expectedUrgency: prompt scouting; severity depends on crop-wide distribution and confirmed injury
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Inspect adjacent plants, leaf undersides, flowers, and protected sites; avoid claiming the reference species from damage alone.
expectedScoutingSteps: capture a sharp macro of the organism
inspect leaf undersides and flowers for larvae and adults
look for silvering, streaking, scarring, distortion, and black frass
mediaRecords.expectedIpmResponse: Separate direct thrips identification from the causal claim that thrips produced the submitted damage; retain powdery mildew, mites, residue, and physical injury when discriminators are absent.

mediaRecords.lifeStage: adult/immature mites; exact host-view life stages not independently recorded
mediaRecords.affectedLocation: leaf surfaces and fine webbing zones
mediaRecords.distribution: direct mite morphology in macro reference and a separate host infestation view
diagnosticSigns: direct two-spotted spider-mite morphology
fine webbing associated with host tissue
colony-scale host context
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Require direct mites or eggs under magnification, or compatible stippling plus fine mite webbing; do not diagnose from pale marks alone.
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Inspect neighboring plants and avoid moving infested plant material until distribution is understood.
expectedScoutingSteps: inspect leaf undersides with magnification
look for mites, round eggs, cast skins, stippling, and fine webbing
distinguish fine colony webbing from an ordinary spider web
mediaRecords.expectedIpmResponse: Favor spider mites only when direct organism/egg evidence or the combined stippling-and-fine-webbing pattern is present; retain thrips, residue, and physical injury otherwise.

mediaRecords.plant: banana and an additional garden host
mediaRecords.lifeStage: aphid colonies with mixed visible sizes; beneficial adult predator present in comparison view

diagnosticSigns: clustered soft-bodied aphid morphology
multiple aphid sizes in a colony
beneficial lady beetle predation context
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Confirm live soft-bodied aphids and colony distribution; separately classify predators, cast skins, and parasitoid mummies rather than counting every visible insect as a pest.
mediaRecords.expectedUrgency: assess colony size, plant stress, honeydew, and spread before choosing a response
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Inspect adjacent plants and protected growth sites while preserving identified beneficial predators.

look for live colonies, honeydew, cast skins, and distorted growth
separate predators and parasitoid mummies from active aphids
mediaRecords.expectedIpmResponse: Report aphids only from direct colony/body evidence; explicitly identify beneficial predator context and avoid recommending actions that indiscriminately remove beneficials.

mediaRecords.progression: photographed after herbicide injury; timing and recovery not recorded
mediaRecords.environment: field conditions; weather and application conditions not recorded

distorted and injured foliage without direct pest bodies
multiple views from the documented injury set
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Require product, concentration, coverage, application time, light/temperature, and symptom-onset history; do not infer the chemical or active ingredient from appearance.
mediaRecords.expectedUrgency: stop repeat exposure and document the event before recommending any corrective action
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Do not label chemical injury contagious; separately scout for pests or disease when direct signs exist.

compare protected and exposed tissue
record product, rate, timing, weather, light, and symptom onset
inspect for direct mites, eggs, webbing, frass, colonies, or fungal growth

mediaRecords.plant: poison ivy autumn foliage and an unidentified fallen leaf
mediaRecords.lifeStage: seasonal autumn change and fully senesced fallen tissue
mediaRecords.distribution: seasonal coloration and isolated dead fallen tissue; whole-plant distribution is incompletely represented
mediaRecords.progression: seasonal progression is described for the autumn foliage; the fallen leaf is an endpoint only
diagnosticSigns: season-linked red autumn foliage
fully senesced fallen leaf
absence of documented pest bodies, colonies, webbing, frass, or fungal growth
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Require crop stage, season, older-versus-new tissue distribution, progression, and absence of spreading diagnostic signs; color alone cannot prove normal senescence.
mediaRecords.expectedUrgency: low only when timing and distribution support normal aging and no spreading signs exist
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Do not recommend quarantine for normal senescence; escalate only if direct contagious signs or unexpected spread appear.
expectedScoutingSteps: compare old and new growth
record crop stage, season, and progression
inspect lesion margins, undersides, roots, and nearby plants for contradictory signs
mediaRecords.expectedIpmResponse: Treat senescence as a context-dependent hypothesis, not a photo-only diagnosis; avoid pest, disease, or deficiency certainty without distribution, progression, and supporting evidence.

mediaRecords.plant: hibiscus and USDA reference host context
mediaRecords.lifeStage: visible mealybug colonies; exact mixed life stages not independently recorded
mediaRecords.distribution: clustered wax-covered insects rather than a flat powder across leaf tissue
diagnosticSigns: segmented insect bodies beneath wax
clustered colonies in protected sites
distinct body-scale wax rather than continuous fungal growth
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Require sharp body morphology beneath wax and colony placement; inspect for movement, honeydew, crawlers, and attached scale structures before choosing the pest class.
mediaRecords.expectedUrgency: prompt inspection of protected sites and nearby plants
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Limit plant movement while checking spread, but preserve beneficial lookalikes until identified.
expectedScoutingSteps: inspect buds, nodes, petioles, leaf undersides, and container edges
capture a sharp macro showing body segmentation and wax filaments
look for honeydew, ants, crawlers, and attached scale covers
mediaRecords.expectedIpmResponse: Do not call white material powdery mildew when discrete wax-covered bodies are visible; do not call mealybugs when only flat white marks or residue are present.

mediaRecords.distribution: adults and sessile nymphs on foliage; plant-wide distribution not recorded
diagnosticSigns: small white winged adult morphology
flattened whitefly nymphs attached to leaf tissue
beneficial lacewing larva predation context
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Inspect leaf undersides for attached nymphs and sharp adult morphology; use gentle disturbance only as supporting evidence, and separately classify predators rather than counting them as pests.
mediaRecords.expectedUrgency: promptly assess nymph density, honeydew, plant stress, and spread
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Inspect nearby plants and limit movement when multiple life stages are confirmed while preserving lacewings and other identified beneficials.
expectedScoutingSteps: inspect multiple leaf undersides for adults, nymphs, and eggs
photograph attached nymphs and adults sharply at body scale
check for honeydew, sooty growth, cast skins, and distribution
separate lacewings and other predators from pest counts
mediaRecords.expectedIpmResponse: Require direct adult or nymph evidence before calling whiteflies; distinguish attached nymphs from scale and distinguish beneficial lacewing larvae from pests.

leafminer larva associated with the mine
intact outer leaf surfaces around mined tissue
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Confirm that damage is between the leaf surfaces and look for a larva or frass within an active mine; a pale or brown patch alone is insufficient.

compare active translucent mine edges with old necrotic tissue
inspect multiple leaves and nearby plants for distribution
capture both a whole-leaf pattern view and a sharp mine close-up

fixed body-scale structures rather than flat residue
leaf necrosis associated with heavy infestation

mediaRecords.plant: unidentified fruiting plant material in verified Botrytis observations
mediaRecords.lifeStage: senescing or infected reproductive tissue; crop stage not recorded
mediaRecords.distribution: localized gray fungal growth and decaying tissue; whole-plant distribution not recorded
mediaRecords.progression: established mold shown; onset and rate not recorded
mediaRecords.environment: outdoor observations; humidity, airflow, and wetness duration not recorded
diagnosticSigns: gray fuzzy sporulating growth associated with decaying tissue
localized tissue collapse or rot beneath fungal growth
two independently verified Botrytis cinerea observation images
plausibleAlternatives: other saprophytic mold on dead tissue
physical damage followed by secondary colonization
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Confirm gray sporulation arising from actively collapsing tissue and collect environment and progression context; species-level confirmation may require microscopy, culture, or laboratory testing.
mediaRecords.expectedUrgency: prompt isolation and inspection when active rot is suspected, especially in dense or humid reproductive tissue
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Limit contact and movement of suspect material, inspect adjacent tissue, and avoid spreading spores; follow crop-appropriate sanitation rules.
expectedScoutingSteps: inspect inside and outside affected reproductive tissue without contaminating healthy sites
capture sharp views of the gray growth, lesion boundary, and underlying tissue collapse
record humidity, airflow, recent wetness, temperature, and progression
compare nearby healthy and affected tissue and check for wounds or dead material
mediaRecords.expectedIpmResponse: Use these images to recognize generic Botrytis evidence, not to assert cannabis bud rot from visual similarity alone. Require crop-specific tissue views and internal rot evidence before a cannabis bud-rot conclusion, and distinguish gray sporulation from flat powdery residue or normal fading.

imageSet.attributionText: Kava wilt associated with documented Pythium splendens root rot by Scot Nelson, CC0 1.0.

mediaRecords.distribution: individual wilted plants in documented Pythium splendens cases
mediaRecords.progression: endpoint wilt shown; onset and rate not recorded
diagnosticSigns: whole-plant wilt in cases documented as Pythium splendens
loss of turgor compatible with impaired root function
no visible root lesion, discoloration, sloughing, or pathogen structure in the submitted views
plausibleAlternatives: waterlogging or low root-zone oxygen without confirmed pathogen
root aphids or other root pests
vascular wilt or other root pathogens
mediaRecords.confirmationMethod: Inspect washed roots and crown, record substrate moisture, temperature, oxygenation or drainage, and irrigation history, and confirm Pythium with culture, microscopy, or an appropriate test when species-level certainty matters.
mediaRecords.expectedUrgency: prompt root-zone inspection when wilt persists despite appropriate moisture
mediaRecords.expectedQuarantineGuidance: Avoid sharing runoff, tools, or root-zone material until contagious root disease is excluded; do not label ordinary transient wilt contagious without supporting evidence.
expectedScoutingSteps: photograph washed healthy and affected roots plus the crown transition
record irrigation timing, substrate moisture, drainage, root-zone temperature, and oxygenation context
inspect for discoloration, sloughing, odor, root insects, and vascular symptoms
compare affected and unaffected plants and obtain a pathogen test when consequences are high
mediaRecords.expectedIpmResponse: Treat wilt as compatible with root dysfunction but not diagnostic of Pythium. Do not confirm root rot from foliage alone, do not invent a pathogen treatment, and request root images, root-zone measurements, irrigation history, and confirmatory testing.
